title: API 653 Training in San Francisco: Tank Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 653 exam prep for Bay Area tank inspectors: Richmond, Selby and Concord terminals, breakout tanks, Air District seal rules. Instructor Q&A.
h1: API 653 Training in the San Francisco Bay Area: Online Exam Prep for Terminal, Pipeline and Refinery Tank Inspectors
html:
API 653 exam prep for tank inspectors around San Francisco Bay

Much of the Bay Area's fuel moves through tanks that never belong to a refinery: terminals on the Richmond waterfront and the Carquinez Strait, pipeline stations inland at Concord, and distribution terminals as far south as San Jose. Add the refinery tank farms at Richmond and Martinez and the feedstock tanks of the renewable fuels plants, and the region needs a steady supply of inspectors who can work through API 653 and API 650 with confidence. This page is for them and for those working towards it: tank NDT technicians, terminal operations staff, tank builders' welders and the engineers who approve repairs.

There is no Atlantis classroom in the San Francisco Bay Area where tank candidates could sit lessons, and there is no Atlantis office in San Francisco, Oakland, Richmond or Concord; Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad, and the API 653 course is self-paced online study, with an instructor who answers your questions from the code text. The American Petroleum Institute sets eligibility, administers the examination in person at Prometric test centres and issues the certification, and you apply to API yourself. Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider.

Terminals and tank farms around the bay

Operators publish more about their tanks than most candidates realise, and the figures show the range of work a Bay Area tank inspector can expect.

Site, as the operator lists itStorage and tanksWhat it handles
Kinder Morgan Richmond Products Terminal533,900 barrels in 43 tanks of 4,725 to 98,808 barrelsCARB gasoline and diesel, ethanol, biodiesel and renewable diesel; one ship dock
Kinder Morgan Richmond Chemical Terminal639,271 barrels in 136 tanks of 714 to 55,000 barrelsChemicals, oilseeds, lubes and waxes; one dock
Sunoco LP Selby Terminal, Crockett2,639,000 barrels in 22 tanks of 14,000 to 200,000 barrelsGasoline, distillate, renewables, avgas and ethanol; one berth and rail
IMTT RichmondAbout 700,000 barrels in 32 tanksBiodiesel, renewable diesel, ULSD and chemicals; one deepwater berth
Kinder Morgan Brisbane Terminal618,000 barrels in 20 tanksGasoline, diesel, turbine fuel and ethanol, with a turbine fuel line to San Francisco Airport
Kinder Morgan San Jose Terminal1,001,100 barrels in 32 tanksGasoline, diesel, renewable diesel, biodiesel, turbine fuel and ethanol, connected to the San Jose Airport jet fuel line

The Kinder Morgan figures come from its Pacific operations brochure, the Selby figures from Sunoco LP's terminal page and the Richmond figures for IMTT from IMTT's own listing. The refineries keep their own crude, intermediate and product tankage at Richmond and Martinez, and the renewable fuels plants have repurposed theirs: the project description for Rodeo said its marine terminal would take renewable feedstocks in place of crude and gas oils, and Martinez Renewables planned to keep using two existing marine oil terminals. Tanks also stand at Benicia, where Valero has stopped refining but, according to E&E News, said it would keep importing gasoline to the Bay Area in the near term.

Breakout tanks at the Concord pipeline hub

Concord is where much of the region's pipeline system starts. Kinder Morgan's brochure describes the breakout facility at its Concord station as the origin of four lines, the North, Bradshaw, Fresno and San Jose lines, with the North Line running through the Sacramento area to a breakout at Rocklin that serves Chico and Reno, while Richmond and Amorco stations feed the Bay Area lines. Federal pipeline rules define a breakout tank as one that relieves surges in a pipeline system or receives and stores product for reinjection into the pipeline, which makes it pipeline equipment as well as a tank.

Under 49 CFR 195.432, operators inspect the physical integrity of in-service atmospheric and low-pressure steel aboveground breakout tanks according to API 653, and tanks built to API 2510 according to section 6 of API 510. The once-a-calendar-year inspection in paragraph (a), at intervals not exceeding 15 months, applies to the breakout tanks that are not inspected under those two paragraphs. The rule also says the risk-based inspection procedures in API 653 section 6.4.3 cannot be used to set a breakout tank's internal inspection interval. In June 2026 PHMSA published a proposed rule that would allow risk-based intervals with a maximum of 20 years for the initial internal inspection and 25 years after that, and would update the incorporated edition of API 653. It remained a proposal when this page was written, so inspect to the rule as it stands and keep an eye on the docket.

What the Bay Area Air District checks on a floating roof

Tank inspectors here meet a second set of inspections that have nothing to do with shell thickness. The Bay Area Air District, which shortened its public name from the Bay Area Air Quality Management District in January 2025, regulates emissions from organic liquid storage under Regulation 8, Rule 5. Its requirements fall on the operator:

  • External floating roofs: the whole circumference of the primary and secondary seals and the roof fittings inspected twice each calendar year, four to eight months apart, and whenever a seal is installed or repaired; tanks under enhanced monitoring more often.
  • Internal floating roofs: the outermost seal and fittings visually inspected twice a year, and the seals inspected for compliance at intervals not exceeding 10 years.
  • Gap limits for primary and secondary seals, and a report certifying compliance sent to the District no later than 60 days after each inspection.
  • Degassing before cleaning through an abatement device, written notice at least three days ahead, and continued degassing until the organic concentration is below 10,000 ppm as methane.

None of this replaces an API 653 inspection, and an API 653 inspection does not satisfy it. The two meet at the same moments, though: the roof and seal condition an air inspector records can be an early sign of a sticking roof or a damaged shell, and a tank coming out of service for its API 653 internal inspection is degassed under the District's rule before anyone enters it. Types of roofs and seals, and the ways they deteriorate, also appear in the API 653 Body of Knowledge.

Changing what a tank holds: renewable feedstocks and the shell formula

Bay Area terminals and plants have been moving tanks into renewable service, and the API 653 Body of Knowledge lists change-of-service effects on suitability for continued service as an exam topic. The clearest effect is in the minimum thickness formula, because its G term is the specific gravity of the stored liquid. These figures are for practice only.

A tank 140 ft in diameter has a maximum liquid level of 44 ft and has stored gasoline, taken in the problem as G = 0.74. The owner wants to store a vegetable oil feedstock with G = 0.92. The bottom course has an allowable stress S of 23,600 psi given in the problem and E = 1.0. Its lowest average thickness is 0.575 in., the corrosion rate is 0.003 in. per year and the next inspection is ten years away, so the problem asks you to judge the thickness expected at that inspection: 0.575 − 0.030 = 0.545 in.

  • Gasoline: tmin = 2.6 (H − 1) D G ÷ (S E) = 2.6 × 43 × 140 × 0.74 ÷ 23,600 = 0.491 in. The course passes.
  • Vegetable oil: the same course needs 2.6 × 43 × 140 × 0.92 ÷ 23,600 = 0.610 in. At 0.545 in. it fails at the full fill height.
  • Maximum fill height in the new service: H = S E t ÷ (2.6 D G) + 1 = 23,600 × 0.545 ÷ 334.88 + 1 = about 39.4 ft.

The owner can lower the operating level by about four and a half feet, repair the course or choose a lighter product for that tank. Temperature can matter as well, because heated storage can bring different design and inspection considerations, so a full change-of-service review looks beyond the arithmetic. Exam questions often state the new product's specific gravity once in the narrative and expect you to notice it.

Linings, cathodic protection and the floor

Two recommended practices in the API 653 Body of Knowledge do much of their work at terminals like these. RP 651 covers cathodic protection of aboveground storage tank bottoms, and RP 652 covers linings of tank bottoms. A terminal inspector reads rectifier and survey records, checks whether a release prevention barrier or new bottom has changed what the cathodic protection can reach, and decides whether a lining failure explains the product-side pitting on a floor scan. The exam tests the concepts, such as which tanks benefit from cathodic protection, the limits a liner places on it, and when a lining is worth applying. API 653's floor rules then turn those observations into minimum remaining thickness and an interval.

Product mix matters too. Fuel ethanol, which the Richmond, Brisbane and Selby terminals all list, is linked in RP 571 to ethanol stress corrosion cracking of carbon steel, a mechanism on the API 653 list, and tanks that switch between gasoline, ethanol, biodiesel and renewable diesel need service records clear enough that the next inspector knows what the shell and floor have seen.

Routes into API 653 from Bay Area tank work

Annex D of API 653 sets the eligibility scale: one year of tank experience including supervision or performance of inspection with a bachelor's degree in engineering or technology, two years with a two-year degree or certificate, three with a high school diploma and five or more without formal education, gained in the last 10 years. The longer routes accept experience in the design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of aboveground storage tanks, with at least a year of inspection. The API 653 certification requirements page has the detail. Typical routes here:

  • Terminal operations staff who gauge, transfer and maintain tanks and have moved into inspection support.
  • Tank NDT technicians who have scanned floors and measured shells and nozzles. The NDT training in the San Francisco Bay Area page covers ASNT method training.
  • Welders and foremen from tank construction and repair contractors. The AWS CWI exam prep for the Bay Area page covers the welding inspector route that many combine with API 653.
  • Engineers in terminal integrity and refinery inspection groups.

Studying API 653 from the Bay Area

API 650 is where many candidates lose time. The open-book questions send you into it for weld spacing, nozzle details, materials and the design and hydrotest formulas, while the closed-book questions lean on API 653's inspection, evaluation and repair rules and on RP 575. Learn API 653 first, then API 650's structure, then RP 571, RP 575, RP 577, RP 651, RP 652 and the parts of Section V and Section IX the Body of Knowledge lists, using the editions on the effectivity sheet for your window. The API 653 tank inspection guide and the API 653 summary help with the big picture.

Terminal work rarely stops for long, and the course is built to be picked up and put down: study when the shift allows, send the instructor the questions that come up on the job, such as a settlement survey that will not fit the Annex B figures or a floor reading you cannot place in the tables. When you schedule, choose a Prometric centre and an appointment time that do not depend on a clear run across the Bay Bridge or Carquinez Bridge at rush hour.

Sponsoring tank inspectors at a Bay Area terminal or plant

Terminal operators, pipeline companies, refineries and tank contractors can enrol several candidates together, and each works at their own pace with the instructor. Fees are quoted on request. Check each person's experience against Annex D before enrolling, because the course does not change eligibility, and mention whether any of the group are aiming at API 570 for dock and manifold piping or API 510 for pressurised storage. The API 653 training overview explains the course content.

faq.q: Are the breakout tanks at the Concord pipeline station inspected to API 653?
faq.a: Under 49 CFR 195.432, in-service atmospheric and low-pressure steel aboveground breakout tanks are inspected according to API 653, and tanks built to API 2510 according to section 6 of API 510. The owner decides who performs those inspections and which certifications it requires. Remember that the federal rule, not only API 653, governs these tanks, including the current bar on using API 653's risk-based procedures to set the internal interval.

faq.q: Can a pipeline operator use RBI to set internal inspection intervals for breakout tanks?
faq.a: Not under the current rule, which says the risk-based procedures in API 653 section 6.4.3 cannot be used to set a breakout tank's internal interval. In June 2026 PHMSA proposed allowing risk-based intervals with maximums of 20 years for the first internal inspection and 25 years afterwards. That was a proposal, not a final rule, when this page was written, so check the current text of the regulation before planning on it.

faq.q: Does the Bay Area Air District require an API 653 inspector for seal inspections?
faq.a: No. Regulation 8, Rule 5 places the seal and fitting inspections on the tank operator and sets their frequency, gap limits and reporting, but it does not require API 653 certification. The rule protects air quality; API 653 protects the tank's integrity. Many terminals use the same people for both, and an API 653 inspector who understands the air rule is easier to schedule around a tank's out-of-service period.

faq.q: Does storing vegetable oil or tallow instead of gasoline change a tank's minimum thickness?
faq.a: Yes. The specific gravity G sits in API 653's shell thickness formula, so a heavier product raises the minimum thickness at the same fill height, or lowers the maximum fill height for the same shell. Heated storage can add other considerations as well. The API 653 Body of Knowledge lists change-of-service effects on suitability for continued service, so expect at least one question built around it.

faq.q: Are the small tanks at the Richmond chemical terminal API 653 tanks?
faq.a: Some may be and some may not. API 653 is written for carbon and low-alloy steel tanks built to API 650 or its predecessor, and many small chemical tanks are shop-built, made of other materials or built to other standards. The owner's tank list and the original construction records decide which standard each tank is inspected to, so check them before you accept a scope at a mixed terminal.

faq.q: Is there an API 653 class I can attend in person in the Bay Area?
faq.a: Not with Atlantis: there is no Atlantis classroom in the San Francisco Bay Area, and the API 653 course is self-paced online study with instructor Q&A. That suits terminal shift patterns and unplanned tank outages. Whichever way you prepare, API holds the examination in person at a Prometric test centre after it accepts your application, and you choose the centre when you schedule.

faq.q: Where do Bay Area candidates sit the API 653 exam?
faq.a: In person at a Prometric test centre; Prometric lists test centres in and around the Bay Area. The exam has 170 questions, 110 closed-book and 60 open-book, over a 7.5-hour day with a lunch break, and the code PDFs are provided on the computer for the open-book part. Personal books and notes stay outside. For window dates and application deadlines, see the API exam schedule page.

faq.q: Can our terminal company sponsor a group of tank inspectors for API 653?
faq.a: Yes. Terminal operators, pipeline companies and contractors can enrol groups, and fees are quoted on request. Each candidate studies at their own pace and applies to API individually with their own experience record. Tell us how many candidates, which exam window they are aiming for and whether any of them also need API 570 or API 510 when you enquire.
